_comment: Innovation proposals — a concept a worker found worth cooking, not a bug fix. Nothing here is implemented from the proposal alone; it has to move through the status lifecycle. Never discard an entry for being 'not immediately useful' -- park it with a reason instead of deleting it.

entry_schema.hypothesis: the falsifiable claim, e.g. 'X currently fails at Y; with Z it succeeds' -- not 'would be cool'
entry_schema.originating_agent: model + task_key of the worker that proposed it
entry_schema.supporting_evidence: what grounds this in an actual observed failure mode -- a scenario-suite result, a ledger entry, a named pattern from comparable tools
entry_schema.estimated_upside: concrete and bounded, not a multiplier -- what measurably improves and by roughly how much, with the honesty that this is a pre-benchmark estimate
entry_schema.dependencies: what this needs to exist first
entry_schema.experiment_required: the specific benchmark or adversarial test that would confirm or kill it
entry_schema.status_reason: required whenever status is rejected or parked -- why, so it can be revisited if the reason stops applying

entries.hypothesis: A priority-ordered, character-budget-aware pruning pass over the DOM/AX snapshot (focused/invalid fields+alerts first, then actionable controls, then repeated records breadth-first, then named sections, then low-value text, with a recoverable omission marker) reduces per-step tokens without losing actionable elements, on pages currently producing oversized snapshots.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator, from reading agentrhq/webcmd (competitive analysis, docs/agent-notes/competitive-analysis.md)
entries.supporting_evidence: webcmd cites this as one of three changes behind its BU Bench V1 token/accuracy numbers versus browser-use -- self-reported, not yet independently reproduced, but the technique itself is inspectable in their public writeup
entries.estimated_upside: unmeasured -- webcmd claims ~10% fewer tokens than browser-use in their run; ours would need its own measurement, not theirs
entries.implementation_cost: medium -- touches the DOM serialization path some existing tests already cover; needs its own scenario coverage before landing
entries.dependencies: the local failure-scenario suite (planned, not yet built) to have a real before/after to measure against
entries.experiment_required: reproduce BU Bench V1 (or a subset) against current browser-use to get OUR baseline numbers first, before building anything -- a prototype without that baseline cant be judged

entries.hypothesis: Returning a structural diff of page state after a browser-run program (instead of a fresh full snapshot), with an explicit opt-out for research-style tasks, reduces tokens on form-filling/multi-step workflows without losing the agent visibility into what changed.
entries.supporting_evidence: same source as above; webcmd explicitly reran both task categories to check the opt-out did not regress research-task accuracy before shipping it
entries.implementation_cost: medium-high -- needs a real diffing strategy against this repo own snapshot format, plus the same before/after discipline webcmd applied (rerun both task types, not just the one being optimized)
entries.dependencies: the failure-scenario suite; also depends on idea 1 if snapshot pruning changes the format being diffed
entries.experiment_required: a scenario/benchmark showing token reduction on multi-step form tasks with zero regression on research-style tasks

entries.hypothesis: Encouraging more aggressive batched code-based execution (multiple browser steps in one agent turn) measurably lowers agent-turns-per-task, the same lever webcmd attributes part of its turn-count advantage to.
entries.supporting_evidence: webcmd states this as one of three factors behind its 9.8-vs-14.8 turns/task number; this repo already has a code-execution-over-page action per its own project history, so the question is usage rate, not whether the capability exists
entries.estimated_upside: unmeasured -- needs a baseline read of how often the existing action is actually invoked vs single-step actions across a real task sample

Requires new instrumentation + a real task corpus before this can even be measured, let alone acted on. Revisit if/when either exists.

entries.title: Watch a video from its pixels: in-page signatures, best-first seek-bisection, contact-sheet handoff
entries.hypothesis: An agent can recover the visual content of a video (what was shown, when it changed) for ~1/250th of the image tokens of a screenshot-per-second, by (a) seeking the <video> instead of playing it, (b) comparing 8x8 in-page thumbnails so the search moves no pixels, (c) spending samples only on the largest changes up to a keyframe budget, and (d) handing the model one contact sheet with timestamps burned in instead of N images.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator (Claude Sonnet 5.5) in response to the owner's request for a low-token, from-pixels video viewer; adversarial review by claude-opus (see findings-log, Round 4)
entries.supporting_evidence: Ground truth: a real WebM with cuts at exactly 2/4/6s and a box moving through every scene - cuts located within one min_gap, motion inside a shot produces zero false cuts (mutation-tested: threshold 0 breaks the motion test, threshold 95 breaks the cut tests). Real video: Big Buck Bunny (9:56, H.264, archive.org) watched in 124 seeks / ~42s wall clock, 8 keyframes, contact sheet 1300x372 (~645 tokens by the published w*h/750 area rule) vs ~183k tokens for a screenshot per second at the same resolution.
entries.estimated_upside: Token figures are ESTIMATES from the published area formula, not measured billing; I attempted a measurement through this session's own token counter and it moved ~163 tokens for the image read, far below the 645 the formula predicts, so that counter cannot validate the estimate and I am not claiming either figure is the true cost. The ~250x ratio is sheet-vs-1fps-screenshots and depends entirely on that baseline being the one you would otherwise use.
entries.implementation_cost: small - one module (browser_use/vision/video.py ~400 lines) reusing live.py's frame_signature/signature_distance; overlay and recorder are separate small modules.
entries.dependencies: a Chromium that can decode the video's codec (the default Playwright build cannot decode H.264; /usr/local/bin/chromium could); Pillow.
entries.experiment_required: NOT DONE: (1) accuracy across several real videos of different kinds (talking head, slides, sports, screencast) against a labelled set of scene boundaries; (2) head-to-head against PySceneDetect / ffmpeg scene filter on the same videos for cut F1 and cost; (3) a task-level test - can a model answer content questions from the sheet as well as from dense frames; (4) a DRM/MSE player (YouTube, Netflix) - untested, and YouTube refused this sandbox with a bot check, so real-player behaviour is unverified.
entries.novelty_assessment: NOT NOVEL as individual techniques: scene-cut detection by thumbnail/histogram differencing (PySceneDetect, ffmpeg scdet), binary search for a change point, storyboard / contact-sheet thumbnails, and canvas drawImage for frame access are all long-established. What is specific here is the COMBINATION aimed at LLM token cost - in-page signatures so the search moves no pixels, best-first refinement that stops at the keyframe budget instead of locating every cut, a min-shot filter, automatic fall-back to screenshots on canvas taint, and a labelled token ledger. That is an engineering recombination; I am not asserting it is patentable or unpublished, and I have not done a prior-art search. Do not cite it as an invention without one.
entries.status_reason: Prototype is working and tested on ground truth plus one real video; it has not been benchmarked against an alternative or across videos, so it does not meet 'benchmarked'.

entries.title: Real-time page scroll distance and position from pixels alone, with self-reported uncertainty
entries.hypothesis: A perception stream can report how far and which way a page scrolled, and keep a running page position, from consecutive screencast frames with no DOM access and no model, in ~10 tokens per tick, and can say when it does not know instead of drifting silently.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator (Claude Sonnet 5.5), prompted by the owner's request to show scrolling with real-time context; gap found by reading perceive._pan
entries.supporting_evidence: Real Wikipedia page, human-style wheel scrolling, ground truth read from window.scrollY: 6 runs, 5 within 0.01h (about 1% of a screen), 1 with one unmeasurable step that the stream flagged uncertain (0.18h off). Before the uncertainty reporting, runs of the same scenario silently lost 1.3-1.9 screens. Unit-level: known-shift and sideways-sprite and repeating-content and weak-match cases, mutation-checked.
entries.estimated_upside: Token figures in the demo HUD are estimates (w*h/750 for the screenshot baseline, len/4 for text); they show a stream of ~300-900 tokens against ~80k for a screenshot per tick, which is a comparison against a baseline nobody sensible would use. The honest value is not the ratio; it is knowing where you are in a page in real time when the DOM is unavailable.
entries.implementation_cost: small - ~100 lines in perceive.py and a few in stream.py, pure Python, no new dependency (numpy is only an optional extra).
entries.dependencies: Pillow; a screencast of the page.
entries.experiment_required: NOT DONE: (1) more sites and page types (sticky-header-heavy, infinite scroll, horizontal, zoomed, dark, image-only); (2) compare with an optical-flow / phase-correlation library on accuracy and CPU; (3) verify the new= strip labels against ground truth; (4) long-run drift behaviour over hundreds of steps; (5) behaviour when screencast frames are dropped under load (partly seen: produces 'unknown').
entries.novelty_assessment: NOT NOVEL. Row-profile / block matching to detect vertical translation is decades old (scroll detection in remote-desktop and screen-sharing codecs, motion estimation in video coding, image stabilisation, phase correlation). What is specific here is only the packaging: a cumulative page position in screens that marks itself uncertain after an unmeasurable step, as a cheap text line for an agent. That is engineering, not an invention, and I have not searched prior art.
entries.status_reason: Works on one site in 6 runs; needs the experiments above before 'benchmarked'.

entries.title: The browser as the agent's eyes and ears: in-page retina, event-gated percepts, verified touch
entries.hypothesis: An agent can follow short-form video (picture and sound, muted or not) for a few hundred tokens per item, with no screenshots and no HTML, by measuring continuously inside the page and sending compressed percepts only when asked or when something salient happens.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator (Opus 5.5), from the owner's request; research sub-agent for streaming-video and capture-API prior art
entries.supporting_evidence: Ground-truth clip through the real browser: cuts within one 10 fps sample, tone 441 Hz for 440, 120 bpm beats, noise and silence located. Real public-domain clips in a local muted feed: all heard, transcripts correct. ~2.5k estimated tokens for ~100 s of video across 5 reels. 19 CI tests.
entries.estimated_upside: Against a screenshot a second at 1280x800 (~1.3k tokens each by the 28 px patch rule) 100 s is ~130k tokens; the percepts were ~2.5k. That baseline is naive; against Gemini-style native video at ~300 tokens/s it is ~30k. The real gain is qualitative: sound and words, cuts, loops, and when to move on, which screenshots do not give at any price.
entries.implementation_cost: done: ~2k lines (retina.js ~500, sight/hearing/percept/service/asr/hook ~1.3k, touch ~200) plus tests.
entries.dependencies: numpy; optional faster-whisper (Silero VAD bundled, Whisper model downloaded on first use).
entries.experiment_required: NOT DONE: (1) Instagram/YouTube/TikTok with a real login in Chrome with proprietary codecs; (2) accuracy of speech/music labels on a labelled set (e.g. GTZAN speech-music, MUSAN) instead of a handful of clips; (3) agent-level A/B: does a Claude session answer questions about reels better and cheaper with eyes_* than with browser_screenshot; (4) per-strip OCR-free readability of on-screen text vs sheet size; (5) CPU cost of the retina on a low-end laptop.
entries.novelty_assessment: NOT NOVEL as techniques (see findings-log Round 6). Specific packaging for a turn-based model; no prior-art search done beyond the research agent's survey.
entries.status_reason: Works end to end on generated and real clips in this sandbox; untested on the target sites.

entries.title: Route choice: direct or Tor with an exit country, for geo-blocked and censored research
entries.hypothesis: Content a network censors or geo-restricts becomes reachable for research/education by routing the browser's SOCKS5 through Tor, without any change to the agent.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator (Opus 4.8), from the owner's request for an app-level fallback transport
entries.supporting_evidence: BrowserProfile.proxy already speaks socks5://; Tor exposes a local SOCKS5 port. Standard control-port NEWNYM (via stem or the raw line protocol) rotates exits with a ~10s cooldown. Shipped as browser_use/net/tor.py with 27 passing pure-logic tests; real-bootstrap test skips when no tor binary present.
entries.estimated_upside: Reaches nationally-censored or geo-fenced pages that otherwise fail at the network layer. Bounded: does NOT help with bot-detection walls (Tor exits are on public blocklists, so Google/YouTube challenge them MORE, not less) — verified against multiple sources.
entries.implementation_cost: Small, done. No new runtime dependency (raw async control client). Off by default.
entries.dependencies: A tor binary on the host, or a Tor the user already runs; obfs4proxy/lyrebird for bridges on censored networks.
entries.experiment_required: End-to-end run on a host with tor installed: bootstrap, fetch a geo-restricted test page, rotate circuit, confirm exit country changes. Not runnable in this sandbox (no tor, egress via fixed proxy).
entries.honest_note: Explicitly not a bot-detection bypass. should_fall_back() refuses to retry CAPTCHAs/unusual-traffic walls through Tor. For YouTube specifically the real paths are the user's own Chrome (--cdp-url) or an alternative frontend (Invidious/Piped).
entries.evidence_update: Round 8: NetworkRouter/TorPool built; one Tor per country because Chromium SOCKS5 has no auth; 30 network tests with real browsers; Chromium verified against a real SOCKS5 proxy (hostname resolved proxy-side, fails closed). Real Tor bootstrap and exit-country verification remain unverified (no tor binary here).
not_built: block images/media in Tor mode (off by default: Retinat is vision-first)
code guard against typing into password fields on Tor
VPS-fleet routing via gost or sing-box (faster and steadier than Tor, costs money, flagged as datacenter)

entries.title: A real browser UI: Chromium/Electron shell a person could switch to from Edge/Brave
entries.hypothesis: The same engine (CDP + eyes + human input + WebMCP synthesis) wrapped in a latest-Chromium chrome with an address bar, tabs and an agent sidebar becomes a browser a person uses day to day, with the agent as a first-class co-pilot in the same window.
entries.originating_agent: owner request (parked for later by owner's own instruction: 'the browser part and the extension part you do this for me later not now')
entries.supporting_evidence: Today browser_use is a library/agent driver with no UI of its own: it drives headless or headful Chromium over CDP, and Retinat/cobrowse are the closest thing to a surface. Comparable OSS to study before building: Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF), Electron, Tauri (Rust/webview), the 'Browser Company' Dia/Arc model, Sidekick, Wavebox, and agent-browsers like Perplexity Comet — for how they mount an agent pane beside real browsing.

entries.experiment_required: Prototype: Electron window loading a real page, eyes sidebar showing percepts live, one agent action from the sidebar acting on the visible tab.
entries.honest_note: This is a product, not a patch. Parked deliberately per owner until the engine-side work (transport, tuning, media) is solid.

entries.title: A companion browser extension (MV3) exposing the engine in the user's existing browser
entries.hypothesis: An MV3 extension in the person's own Chrome/Edge/Brave gives the agent eyes and hands in the browser they already trust and are already logged into — no separate app, no bot-detection problem, because it IS the human's browser.
entries.originating_agent: owner request (parked for later by owner's instruction)
entries.supporting_evidence: An extension runs on the user's real profile and connection, which sidesteps the datacenter-IP flagging entirely. WebMCP synthesis and eyes percepts could be fed from a content script + offscreen document; the native-messaging host bridges to the python engine.

entries.experiment_required: MV3 prototype that captures the active tab's video frames via an offscreen document and streams percepts to the python engine over native messaging.
entries.honest_note: Later, per owner. This — not Tor — is the correct answer to 'don't get flagged': act as the human, with the human, in the human's browser, not disguised as one.

entries.title: Counterfactual re-render attribution: send only the pixels the DOM cannot explain (H(pixels | DOM) percept)
entries.hypothesis: Today the repo's DOM channel and Retinat's pixel channel are redundant and blind in opposite places. DOM-only reports occluded or invisible text as present and misses canvas and image text. A full viewport image (about 1.0-1.8k tokens) pays again for every glyph the DOM already carries. With counterfactual attribution, on a set of mixed local pages the percept should (a) reach planted-fact QA accuracy no lower than the full screenshot (within 3 pp), (b) use at most 40% of the screenshot's image tokens on DOM-heavy pages, and (c) flag at least 90% of planted invisible-but-in-DOM text with under 5% false flags. Falsified if the paint-only intervention shifts layout on more than 5% of pages, if the residual covers more than 60% of the viewport on typical pages (no savings), or if QA accuracy drops by more than 3 pp.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: information-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: The closest work is the hybrid a11y+SoM observation (this repo's DOM side, OmniParser), which sends structure and pixels side by side and leaves the reconciliation to the model. 'Do GUI Agents Believe Their Eyes?' (arXiv 2607.04334) only diagnoses pixel-vs-structure reliance. GDG character grids replace pixels with a text grid. Patch-pruning work (DART, ReVision, AQuaUI, GUIPruner) removes redundancy with heuristic or learned selectors inside the model. None of these uses an interventional re-render: the renderer is queried with do(text colour = transparent) and do(media opacity = 0), so the diff gives the exact causal set of pixels each DOM source produced. This works at the closed-API boundary because it needs no tokenizer access. It also yields a free detector for pixel-structure disagreement (DOM text that is not visible). Searches for counterfactual or masked-render attribution in web agents found nothing; that negative is unverified.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate, unmeasured: a 40-70% cut in image tokens on DOM-heavy pages (most ink is DOM text); about 0% on canvas-only or video-only surfaces, where the whole viewport is residual, and the method should report that honestly. Qualitative gain: a deterministic invisible-text detector that removes a class of DOM-says-yes hallucinations. Costs 2-3 extra frame captures per percept (estimate 60-150 ms).
entries.experiment_required: tests/ci-style, pytest-httpserver, a real Chromium through BrowserSession, no LLM for the core metrics. Build 20 local pages with planted ground truth: DOM paragraphs; a canvas fillText price; a PNG banner with text; a <video> with burned-in caption frames; a WebGL label; DOM text hidden under a fixed modal; text the same colour as its background; overflow-clipped text; ::before generated content. For each page, compute the layout-guard pass rate, the residual area fraction, precision and recall of R against the planted non-DOM text boxes, precision and recall of invisible-DOM flags, and tokens by the 28-px rule against the full viewport. Optional second stage: ask Claude 5 planted-fact questions per page under three conditions (screenshot only, DOM only, attribution percept) and compare accuracy against tokens. Cost: under an hour of compute, about 300 model calls.
entries.mechanism: Inputs: one frozen world state, the DOM (DOMSnapshot with layout boxes and text runs, already produced in browser_use/dom), and the compositor frame (page.py screencast or Page.captureScreenshot fromSurface). Algorithm: (0) Freeze the state. Use Animation.setPlaybackRate(0) plus the existing hold=True video pause, or Emulation.setVirtualTimePolicy('pause') (cdp-use exposes all three), so that renders 1..k show the same instant. (1) F0 = normal frame. (2) Intervene with a paint-only stylesheet added through CSS.createStyleSheet + CSS.setStyleSheetText: `*{color:transparent!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:transparent!important;text-shadow:none!important;caret-color:transparent!important}`, then capture F_t. This is do(text ink = 0). (3) A second intervention, `img,video,canvas,svg,picture{opacity:0!important}` plus background-image:none, gives F_m. (4) Layout guard: take a DOMSnapshot before and after each intervention and abort if any box moves by more than 0.5 px. Colour and opacity should not trigger relayout, and the guard tests that assumption. (5) On the 28x28-px patch grid the host tokenizer uses, attribute each patch: A_text = mean|F0-F_t| > tau (ink belongs to DOM text); A_media = |F0-F_m| > tau. The residual R is the set of patches in F_t that still carry glyph-like high-frequency energy (Laplacian energy above a local MAD threshold) and are not inside a DOM text box. R is text the DOM does not know about: canvas fillText, text baked into images, burned-in video captions, WebGL labels. (6) Inverse check: for each DOM text node whose box has zero attributed ink (F0 equals F_t inside the box), mark it as DOM-claims-visible but pixels-say-invisible (occluded by a modal, clipped by overflow, same colour as the background, opacity 0). Output: the visible DOM text with its boxes, sent as text, with invisible nodes dropped or flagged; residual patches cropped and packed on the 28-px grid; a one-line attribution summary. Rate: R_total = R_text(visible DOM) + sum over residual patches of ceil(w/28)*ceil(h/28). This is conditional coding. A whole screenshot costs about H(X) tokens. This percept costs about H(X|DOM): the DOM channel is sent anyway at text rates, and pixels go only where it leaves uncertainty.

closest_prior_art.name: Do GUI Agents Believe Their Eyes? Diagnosing State-Belief Reliance on Pixels versus Structure (arXiv 2607.04334)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Frames the DOM/a11y channel and the screenshot as redundant channels that can disagree. Uses a re-render control (re-paints the true value into the same region) and proposes a source-aware consistency gate that checks whether the pixels back up the structural label before acting. It diagnoses and gates; it does not encode a percept from an interventional diff, and it does not cut pixel tokens.

closest_prior_art.name: PhantomLint: Principled Detection of Hidden LLM Prompts in Structured Documents (arXiv 2508.17884)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Does the proposal's step (6) inverse check by another route. For each text block it renders the block's minimal region, OCRs the image, and flags extracted text that the OCR does not see (that is, text present in the structure but not visible) on HTML and PDF. The test is render-vs-structure consistency per region, with OCR where the proposal uses a do(color=transparent) diff.

closest_prior_art.name: Google patent US8639680B1 / US9336279 - Hidden text detection for search result scoring
closest_prior_art.overlap: Detects DOM text that will not be shown by diffing the DOM tree against the render tree, and flags text whose colour matches the background or whose font is below a size threshold. Covers part of the 'DOM claims visible, pixels say invisible' detector (off-screen, same colour as background), without pixel-level verification.

closest_prior_art.name: browser-use paint-order filtering (this repo, browser_use/dom/serializer/paint_order.py, DOMSnapshot paintOrders)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The repo already drops DOM elements hidden under higher-paint-order boxes, which is the modal-occlusion case of the inverse check. CDP CSS.getBackgroundColors, as used by contrast checkers, also covers the same-colour-as-background case without a pixel diff.

closest_prior_art.name: SnapGuard: Lightweight Prompt Injection Detection for Screenshot-Based Web Agents (arXiv 2604.25562)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Reads text from screenshot pixels with contrast-polarity reversal and OCR to catch injected text that a structure-only view misses or misrepresents. This is pixel-side text recovery for web agents; it is not counterfactual.

closest_prior_art.name: Brave - Unseeable prompt injections in screenshots (Comet and other AI browsers)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Documents the threat class the residual channel R targets: text that exists only in pixels (faint, in images) and not in the DOM, read by screenshot-reading agents. It motivates pixel-vs-DOM reconciliation.

closest_prior_art.name: A11y-Compressor (arXiv 2605.00551, ACL SRW 2026)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Cuts redundancy in hybrid a11y observations: modal detection, filtering of visually hidden nodes, dedup. It overlaps with dropping invisible or occluded DOM text, but it is rule-based on the tree only, with no image processing or re-render.

closest_prior_art.name: AQuaUI: Visual Token Reduction for GUI Agents with Adaptive Quadtrees (arXiv 2605.19260)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Training-free, layout-driven visual-token reduction for GUI screenshots. It goes after the same 'most pixels are redundant' budget with a content-density heuristic rather than causal attribution to the DOM.

closest_prior_art.name: ShowUI (CVPR 2025) UI-guided visual token selection
closest_prior_art.overlap: Removes about 33% of redundant visual tokens using UI-connected-component structure of the screenshot. This is in-model pruning, so it needs model and tokenizer access, which the proposal avoids.

closest_prior_art.name: Accessibility tree vs screenshots: the token math behind my browser agent (DEV)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Engineering practice: 'snap first, shot last'. Send the a11y tree and fall back to pixels for canvas or when the tree is uncertain. This is the coarse whole-frame version of 'send pixels only where the DOM leaves uncertainty'.

closest_prior_art.name: OCR in Test Automation: Verify Text Your DOM Can't Reach (TestMu AI)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Established QA practice of OCRing screenshot regions to recover text in canvas, images, charts and video captions that DOM locators cannot see. This is the residual-text use case, done by OCR rather than by interventional diff.

closest_prior_art.name: Hide Web Elements Before Capturing Screenshots (CSS injection before capture; also Percy percyCSS / BackstopJS hideSelectors)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Injecting a stylesheet to hide or alter elements before a screenshot is standard visual-testing and screenshot-service practice. The intervention primitive itself (paint-only CSS, then capture and diff) is not new; what is new is using it as a causal attribution operator.

entries.what_remains_new: What I could not find anywhere: using paired paint-only interventional re-renders, do(text ink = transparent) and do(media opacity = 0) captured at a frozen instant with a DOMSnapshot layout guard, as the observation encoder for an LLM web agent. The output would be (a) DOM text sent as text, with visibility checked against the pixels (an ink-diff of zero means the text is flagged invisible), plus (b) only the residual patches the DOM does not explain (canvas fillText, text baked into images or video, WebGL), sized against a patch-token budget. Each piece has prior art. Re-render or OCR consistency checks exist (PhantomLint, 2607.04334). Invisible-text detection by DOM vs render tree exists (Google patent, the repo's own paint_order). CSS injection before capture exists (visual testing). Hybrid a11y+screenshot token cutting exists (A11y-Compressor, AQuaUI, ShowUI). The combination, a deterministic renderer-side counterfactual diff that yields both a causal pixel-to-DOM attribution map and a conditional-rate percept at a closed-API boundary, turned up nothing in 16 searches. The pixel-verified inverse check is also somewhat stronger than tree-based visibility. It catches ancestor opacity, clip-path, filters, mix-blend-mode, and text that is clipped but still has a box, which paint-order and render-tree diffs miss. Treat this negative as unverified: none of the 2026 GUI-efficiency survey's observation section described it, but no full-text patent search was run.
entries.technical_flaws_found:
1) The intervention is not text-only. `*{color:transparent}` also blanks everything that paints with currentColor: borders, outlines, text-decoration, box-shadow defaults, inline SVG icons with fill/stroke=currentColor, and icon fonts. All of that gets attributed to 'DOM text' and dropped as redundant, but an SVG icon's meaning is not in the DOM text channel. `*` also misses pseudo-elements: ::before/::after, ::placeholder, ::marker, ::selection, ::first-letter need their own selectors. Form-control internals (input values, select text, UA shadow DOM) and `-webkit-background-clip:text` gradient text react differently. Emoji and colour fonts (COLR/CBDT) and images inside text may ignore `color`. Elements with `color` set inline !important beat the stylesheet unless it is injected as a user-agent or inspector stylesheet with higher priority.
2) The residual detector is weak. 'Glyph-like high-frequency energy above a local MAD threshold' fires on any texture: photos, icons, gradients with dithering, chart lines, borders. Precision against planted non-DOM text will be poor, and on image-heavy pages R can easily pass the 60% falsifier. Step (3) does not help R either, because R is taken from F_t, which still contains media. To isolate non-DOM text you need an actual text detector (or OCR) on the residual, which takes you back to known OCR-on-residual practice.
3) Freezing is harder than claimed. Animation.setPlaybackRate(0) only freezes CSS and Web Animations. rAF-driven canvas/WebGL, GIF/APNG, video, caret blink and JS timers keep running unless Emulation.setVirtualTimePolicy('pause') is used. Under virtual-time pause, Page.captureScreenshot and screencast frames are known to stall or return stale frames in some Chromium versions, and a paused virtual clock can block the stylesheet change from reaching a new compositor frame. Without a true freeze, any canvas animation shows up as F0-F_t diff and gets misattributed to DOM text.
4) The layout guard checks the wrong thing. Colour and opacity changes do not relayout, but they can change compositing. Opacity 0 on video/canvas can demote layers, change the rasterization path, and shift antialiasing, which produces diff noise. The real risk is the restyle side effects of `!important` overrides and paint-time differences, not box movement, and DOMSnapshot boxes will not catch them.
5) The rate model is mis-specified for the target host. 28-px patches match Qwen2-VL's tokenizer, not Claude, which bills roughly (w*h)/750 tokens per image with per-image overhead and minimum sizes. Packing many small residual crops can cost more than one downscaled screenshot. Cropping also loses spatial context, and DOM text sent without pixels loses styling that carries meaning: red error text, strikethrough prices, disabled grey, emphasis, and which text sits inside which visual card. Planted-fact QA may hold, but action-relevant visual semantics may not.
6) The information-theory framing is loose. H(X|DOM) assumes a decoder that can reconstruct pixels from the DOM. The LLM is not that decoder, so this is not Slepian-Wolf/Wyner-Ziv conditional coding. It is selective transmission, a heuristic about relevance, not a rate bound.
7) The inverse check works, but it duplicates cheaper signals for most cases: paint order (already in the repo), CSS.getBackgroundColors, and DOMSnapshot textColorOpacities and clientRects. Its unique value is the residual cases (ancestor opacity, filters, clip-path, mix-blend-mode, overflow clipping with a non-empty box). Its own false-positive risk: text drawn in the same colour as its background but with a text-shadow or outline, and low-contrast text where |F0-F_t| falls under tau.
8) Cost: 2-3 extra full-frame captures plus 2-4 DOMSnapshots per percept. On heavy pages DOMSnapshot alone often takes over 100 ms, so 60-150 ms is optimistic. 200-600 ms is more realistic.

entries.title: Belief leases: region-anchored, zero-token invalidation of the model's narrated visual memory
entries.hypothesis: An AOI-style persistent narration memory (the strongest known pattern) currently keeps stale or misread facts with no correction: AOI's own limitations note that a misread number persists. Re-looking every turn fixes staleness but costs about 1-1.8k image tokens per turn. Test page: a local dashboard with 6 widgets updating at random times (DOM-text widgets and canvas widgets) and the task 'answer current values of A and B whenever asked; alert when C crosses Y'. Without leases, narration-memory agents should report stale values in at least 30% of queries after a change. With leases the stale rate should fall below 5%, using at most 30% of the image tokens of re-look-every-turn. Locally, without an LLM, against the page's own change log: invalidation recall of at least 0.95, at most 0.05 false breaks per lease-minute on calibrated animated regions, detection latency under 250 ms. Falsified if the noise-floor calibration cannot keep false breaks below that rate on spinners or carets, or if canvas-widget recall falls below 0.9 at the 32x8 grid.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: information-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: AOI (arXiv 2606.29472) keeps narration but never verifies or retracts it. OMCD in 'When Memory Lies' (arXiv 2608.04574) re-audits memory entries with model calls at each decision point, in batches of 10 valid/stale judgments; its authors find the effect depends on the model's own visual grounding, and it spends tokens on every audit. CausalCache (arXiv 2608.22577) invalidates cached GUI state using causal dependencies; I could only read a tool-generated summary of it, so the exact overlap is unverified, and nothing in that summary describes local pixel or DOM witnesses that push between turns. Leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989) and cache-coherence invalidation are old systems ideas. The new part is applying them to perceptual beliefs: per-claim regions, self-calibrated noise floors, a pixel witness and a DOM witness, and grant-time contradiction against the DOM, all running in the eyes at no model-token cost and pushed into a turn-based host. Out of scope: DOM-diffing alone, which misses canvas and video.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate: image tokens per turn on monitoring tasks fall from about 1-1.8k (re-look) to about 0-300 (one crop per invalidation), a 70-95% cut when change is sparse. Stale-fact errors fall from the 30%+ expected under narration-only memory to under 5%. These targets are set before measuring and are unconfirmed. Little or no gain when the whole screen changes every turn, e.g. a feed swipe, where leases lapse at once.
entries.experiment_required: Local pytest-httpserver dashboard page with a JS-logged ground-truth change schedule (timestamps, widget, old and new value), 3 DOM widgets and 3 canvas widgets, plus decoys: a spinner and a blinking caret inside leased boxes, and an animated ad next to them. Phase 1, no LLM: grant leases programmatically on all widgets, run 5 minutes, and compute recall, false-break rate, latency, and the contradiction check against deliberately wrong claimed values. Phase 2, with Claude: compare 3 agent conditions (re-look every turn; narration memory only; narration plus leases) on 50 query points. Measure stale-answer rate and total image tokens by the 28-px rule. A few hours of wall-clock time, about 150-300 model calls.
entries.mechanism: Inputs: claims the host model makes about what it saw, as structured narration from a new Retinat tool remember(claims=[{text, box, value?, volatile?}]) or parsed from a narration field returned with look/watch; the screencast stream (page.py) or the retina ring; the DOM. For each claim c the eyes grant a lease L_c = (box in page coordinates, mapped through scroll offsets or vision/perceive.scroll_estimate; a reference signature s_c of the crop at higher resolution than 16x16, e.g. a 32x8 luma grid for a text line; the DOM nodes intersecting the box, found with DOM.getNodeForLocation; a noise floor). Calibration: during the first ~1 s of the lease, estimate the region's own variability as the median and MAD of d(s_t, s_c), so blinking carets, spinners and gradient ads in the box are calibrated out. Watching between turns, at no model-token cost: (i) pixel witness, d(s_t, s_c) > median + k*MAD sustained over 2 frames; (ii) DOM witness, an isolated-world MutationObserver on characterData and attributes of the leased nodes. Either witness breaks the lease and emits {claim id, t, witness, new small crop of about 100-300 tokens, new DOM text if any}. The event goes out through the existing hook.py ambient line, or wakes the host when the lease was marked watch=true. Contradiction check at grant time: if the leased box overlaps DOM text and the DOM text disagrees with the claimed value (normalised string or number compare), the claim is returned as contradicted at once. This catches misread numbers before they persist, the error AOI names. Expiry: a lease lapses when its box leaves the viewport for longer than T or the URL changes, so a scrolled-away claim is reported unknown, not true. Information view: what is transmitted is the surprise relative to the model's committed beliefs, -log P(observation | belief), instead of relative to pixel history. Pixel change outside leased regions costs zero bits unless a global 'anything new' lease is held. The rate drops to about 0 when nothing the model depends on changes, and each invalidation costs one crop.

closest_prior_art.name: Unjuno/agent-interface: scoped, expiring semantic target handles with revalidation (issue #45)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The closest systems precedent I found. Runtime-owned references to GUI targets carry an expiry and revalidation predicates, and come back VALID/MOVED/MISSING/STALE so the agent does not re-ground every turn. That is a lease on a perceptual reference. The difference is that these handles are for targets of actions, not for values the model narrated, and nothing says a background witness pushes a break between turns.

closest_prior_art.name: Unjuno/agent-interface: fresh contradiction guards on model-facing temporal speculation (issue #2092)
closest_prior_art.overlap: A local, non-LLM guard checks the model-facing state against freshly captured frames and invalidates stale predictions, ending in UNKNOWN/YIELD. This is close to the pixel-witness break and the 'unknown, not true' semantics. It covers motion speculation, not narrated facts.

closest_prior_art.name: Unjuno/agent-interface: source-bound temporal narration (issue #6213)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Every narration clause must cite source frame/event IDs and a validity time, and the text is marked stale or removed when its source is withdrawn. This is AOI-style narration bound to provenance with retraction. It has no live pixel or DOM witness, no noise calibration, and no contradiction check against the DOM.

closest_prior_art.name: Unjuno/agent-interface PR #498: pixel guard plus self-action invalidation evidence
closest_prior_art.overlap: Pixel guards are RGB SHA-256 hashes over fixed regions, used as evidence that an observation is still valid, and an observation loses authority after the agent's own navigation. The authors say plainly that it cannot detect external changes.

closest_prior_art.name: PUSV, Temporal UI State Inconsistency / TOCTOU defense for CUAs (arXiv 2604.18860)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Masked grayscale SSIM on a 160x160 patch at the planned click target (tau=0.92), plus a global diff with a noise floor calibrated for cursor blink and clocks. This re-validates region-anchored visual state before an action. It runs once, just before dispatch, is not tied to the model's claims, and the authors note it is blind to DOM-only changes.

closest_prior_art.name: Visualping area-selection monitoring (and Distill.io visual selector)
closest_prior_art.overlap: A commercial product that monitors a selected region for pixel change with a threshold and an AI filter for noise, then notifies. This is the pixel-witness half as a long-standing product, minus belief binding and minus per-region self-calibration. Distill: https://distill.io/docs/web-monitor/what-is-visual-selector/

closest_prior_art.name: US11962582 display change detector over a defined screen area
closest_prior_art.overlap: A background process periodically captures the bitmap of a specified area, computes a similarity percentage, and fires a notification policy when it crosses a threshold. Prior art for region-anchored pixel witnesses with notification.

closest_prior_art.name: vercel-labs/agent-browser --if-changed / --threshold / diff snapshot
closest_prior_art.overlap: An agent tool that skips unchanged screenshots per tab and selector to save tokens, with a pixel-ratio threshold, plus accessibility-tree diffing scoped to a selector. Change-gated token savings for agents, but pull-based and not tied to claims.

closest_prior_art.name: AgentX event-aware screen capture (issue #83)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Region wait-for-change and wait-for-stable primitives, plus a low-resolution ring buffer for regions, aimed at agents. A region-change trigger with no belief binding.

closest_prior_art.name: When Memory Lies / OMCD (arXiv 2608.04574)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Stale-memory filtering with event-triggered re-audits. Detection is done by LLM calls in batches of 10, in a symbolic 8x8 FrozenLake rather than a GUI. Same problem, but the solution spends model tokens. Vision-mode F1 runs from 0.067 to 0.887, which supports doing detection locally rather than with the model.

closest_prior_art.name: MemTX transactional belief commit (arXiv 2607.23929)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Records carry validity and provenance, and retracting a belief cascades repairs. These are retraction semantics for agent beliefs, but at the text and tool level, with no perceptual witnesses.

closest_prior_art.name: Invalidation Contracts for Cross-Episode Agent Memory (arXiv 2609.00243)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Version stamps and cacheability hints so agents can evict stale memory. Cache coherence applied to agent memory, at the API and schema level rather than perceptual.

closest_prior_art.name: AOI, Agent-Computer Observation Interfaces (arXiv 2606.29472)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The baseline being improved on. Visual narration is kept as text memory with no verification or retraction.

closest_prior_art.name: CausalCache (arXiv 2608.22577)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Low. It chooses which archived screenshots to restore under a budget using learned utility. There is no invalidation logic and no pixel or DOM witnesses, confirmed from the repo README.

closest_prior_art.name: Gray & Cheriton 1989, Leases
closest_prior_art.overlap: Time-bounded leases for cache consistency. The systems idea itself.

closest_prior_art.name: POCD, probabilistic object-level change detection (arXiv 2205.01202)
closest_prior_art.overlap: In robotics, stored map beliefs are invalidated per object by local change evidence with Bayesian stationarity scores. The same idea as per-claim, region-anchored belief invalidation, applied to 3D maps.

entries.what_remains_new:
Every primitive exists on its own: region pixel-change watchers with thresholds (Visualping, US11962582, AgentX, agent-browser), pre-action region SSIM re-validation (PUSV), expiring perceptual handles revalidated by local guards that resolve to UNKNOWN (Unjuno agent-interface #45, #2092, #498), narration bound to sources and withdrawn when they are (Unjuno #6213), belief retraction and cascades (MemTX), and model-based stale audits (OMCD). What I did not find in any single work:
(1) leases granted on facts the model itself narrated (its values and readings), not on targets of actions or on whole pages.
(2) a pixel witness and a DOM witness on the same lease, so canvas widgets and DOM text are covered under one rule.
(3) a per-lease noise floor learned online (median/MAD), so spinners or carets inside the leased box are calibrated out.
(4) a contradiction check at grant time against DOM text, which catches misread numbers before they persist.
(5) a lapse when the box leaves the viewport or the URL changes, so the claim becomes 'unknown' rather than staying true.
(6) breaks pushed into a turn-based MCP host as small crops, with zero model tokens when nothing leased changes.
The novelty is the composition and the target (the model's narrated perceptual beliefs), not any individual mechanism. Unjuno/agent-interface is the work closest to the spirit and should be cited and compared directly. Its handles plus fresh-pixel guards amount to perceptual leases for actions. Extending them to narrated facts, with dual witnesses, is the gap.
entries.technical_flaws_found:
1. A scalar region distance with a MAD floor cannot tell a spinner apart from a value change inside the same box. If the spinner sets the floor, a one-digit canvas change (3 to 8 is a few dozen pixels) falls under it and recall collapses. If the spinner is not calibrated out, it causes false breaks. Fix: a per-cell variance mask. Calibrate each of the 32x8 cells and exclude or down-weight high-variance cells, then threshold the max or sum over stable cells. Also apply an absolute floor, because a static region gives MAD of about 0, so median + k*MAD becomes a hair trigger on JPEG noise.
2. Screencast frames are JPEG at the screencast's scale and arrive only on compositor damage. Quantization noise varies with what changed elsewhere in the frame, so calibration done while the page is quiet does not hold during unrelated repaints. Fix the quality setting and use luma means over cells, not raw pixels.
3. A 1 s calibration window is shorter than common periodic animations: caret blink is about 1.06 s, and carousels and tickers run 3-10 s. These will produce false breaks after calibration. Calibrate over at least 2 periods, or keep updating robust statistics online while the DOM witness is quiet.
4. Layout shift, sticky headers and sub-pixel scroll move the widget without changing its value, so the pixel witness fires. Re-anchor the box every frame from the leased node's getBoundingClientRect (DOM widgets) or from the scroll offset, and only then compare. Canvas widgets have no DOM anchor and are exposed to this.
5. DOM.getNodeForLocation returns the topmost node at one point, not every node intersecting the box. Several points need sampling, or a walk of elementsFromPoint/getClientRects.
6. Watching only characterData and attributes misses React/Vue re-renders that replace text nodes (childList). Observe childList with subtree on a stable ancestor, and break on a change in normalised text, not on any mutation; otherwise same-value re-renders cause false breaks.
7. The grant-time contradiction check can raise false contradictions, because DOM text is not always what is rendered: CSS text-transform, ::before/::after content, overflow ellipsis, visually hidden spans, locale formatting, and number abbreviations such as 1.2k vs 1234. It needs normalisation and a check against rendered text.
8. A turn-based host cannot be woken mid-turn. Hook ambient lines and MCP notifications are only read at the next turn or hook event, as the repo's agent-notes record. 'Push' therefore means the break is ready at the next turn, not a real interrupt. That still fixes staleness, but the 'alert when C crosses Y' latency is bounded by the host's turn cadence, not by the 250 ms the eyes achieve.
9. The -log P(observation | belief) framing is decoration. The mechanism is a thresholded change detector with no likelihood model, so it should not be presented as a rate-optimal code.
10. The 30% stale-rate baseline depends on how often queries fall after changes, so it should be stated relative to the change schedule.
11. A 250 ms latency target at 2-frame confirmation needs at least 8 fps of screencast. That holds for animated canvas pages, but on a quiet page frames arrive only on damage, which is actually favourable.

entries.title: Error-controlled virtual-time stepping: adaptive temporal refinement so a slow model sees sub-300 ms events frame-exactly
entries.hypothesis: Every observe-act loop today misses or reacts too late to sub-300 ms events. At AOI's ~3 Hz, the chance of catching a 120 ms flash is about 0.36, and with a 2 s model turn the chance of clicking while the target is still visible is about 0. ABP and VideoGameBench Lite pause between steps but still sample only at step boundaries. On a local canvas page that shows 120 ms targets at random times (~20/min), error-controlled virtual-time stepping should detect at least 98% of targets and let the model click inside the target window on at least 90% of them. It should use at most 20% of the frames that fixed 1-frame stepping needs for the same recall. Falsified if virtual time does not govern rAF and canvas timing in the repo's Chromium build, if per-step overhead exceeds about 80 ms so that a 60 s episode becomes impractically slow, or if the controller's recall at a fixed frame budget is no better than uniform sampling at that budget.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: information-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: Agent Browser Protocol (github.com/theredsix/agent-browser-protocol) freezes JS and virtual time between agent actions and captures one settled frame per step, with no intra-step sampling or step-size control. VideoGameBench Lite (arXiv 2505.18134) pauses the emulator during inference, again with step-boundary observation only. Headless --virtual-time-budget is used for deterministic rendering, not perception. Swift Sampling (arXiv 2605.22678) uses Taylor-extrapolation error to choose frames from an already recorded video, offline and in feature space. The new combination is putting that prediction-error estimator in the loop as a step-size controller on the page's own clock, so the eyes choose when the world is sampled, plus the 'advance until surprise, then hold' action. AOI explicitly lists sub-300 ms and real-time games as out of scope, and none of the above closes that gap with frame-exact sampling for a closed-API model. Searches found no adaptive virtual-time stepping for agents; that negative is unverified.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate: detection of 120 ms events rises from ~36% (3 Hz) to over 95%, and in-window reaction from ~0% to over 90% with a 2 s deliberating model, using about 5x fewer frames than fixed 1-frame stepping on sparse-event content. Wall-clock grows by about 3-6x per virtual second while stepping, as an estimate, so this suits tasks that can afford slow-motion, such as testing your own app or game, and not live or server-clocked content.
entries.experiment_required: Local pytest-httpserver page: a canvas rAF loop that draws a target for 120 ms at Poisson times, logs ground truth by performance.now (virtual), and records clicks. Conditions: (a) real-time screencast plus the existing eyes at their natural rate; (b) ABP-style pause only at step boundaries with fixed h = 333 ms; (c) fixed h = 16.7 ms; (d) the adaptive controller. Measure detection recall, frames captured, wall-clock per virtual second and per-step CDP overhead. Then add a scripted 'model' that waits 2 s of wall-clock per decision and clicks the detected target (no LLM needed), and measure the hit rate inside the window. Also check whether Date.now and performance.now freeze under 'pause', and run the same pages with a <video> to record the media behaviour. Under an hour.
entries.mechanism: Inputs: a page whose dynamics run on the renderer's clock (timers, rAF, CSS/Web Animations, canvas and WebGL loops, Date and performance.now); the 16x16 luma signatures already computed by page.py and sight.py. Freeze: Emulation.setVirtualTimePolicy(policy='pause'), exposed in cdp-use. Step: setVirtualTimePolicy(policy='advance', budget=h, waitForNavigation semantics with pauseIfNetworkFetchesPending), wait for Emulation.virtualTimeBudgetExpired, capture the frame (screencast latest, or HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame under begin-frame control for an exact committed frame), and reduce it to signature g_n. Local error estimator, an embedded predictor in the style of adaptive ODE integrators: g_hat_{n} = g_{n-1} + (h_n/h_{n-1})(g_{n-1} - g_{n-2}), a first-order Taylor step on the signature trajectory, and e_n = ||g_n - g_hat_n|| / noise. Controller: h_{n+1} = h_n * clamp(safety * (tol/e_n)^(1/2), 0.25, 2), bounded to [h_min = one frame (16.7 ms), h_max]. Each sample with e_n > tol is marked as an event and its JPEG is kept for the percept. A real event cannot be rewound, but because the world is frozen between steps the controller loses nothing by shrinking h after the first surprising sample: the next frames of a 120 ms event are captured at 1-frame resolution. Agent-facing actions: advance(until='surprise', max=T) runs the controller until an event, then leaves the page paused on that exact frame; act_at(action) injects input at the current frozen virtual instant and then resumes stepping. Output: an event timeline in virtual ms, keyframes chosen by prediction error instead of coverage, and the world paused while the model deliberates. Information view: samples are allocated in proportion to the local bandwidth of the signal (adaptive, near-Nyquist sampling), which approaches constant surprise per sample. The real-time rate constraint (bits per wall-second, which a 2-5 s model turn cannot meet) becomes a bits-per-turn constraint. Out of scope: anything server-timed or multiplayer. Unverified: whether HTMLMediaElement playback follows virtual time; <video> keeps the repo's existing seek or hold path.

closest_prior_art.name: Agent Browser Protocol (ABP), Chromium fork
closest_prior_art.overlap: Freezes JS, timers, Date.now and virtual time between agent actions so the page waits while the model thinks. It has pause/resume and virtual-time control endpoints and auto-captures a compositor screenshot after each settled action. It does no intra-step sampling and no step-size control. So the 'world paused while the model deliberates' half of the idea is already shipped for browsers.

closest_prior_art.name: WaterUI MCP 'advance' tool (PR #823)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The closest match. It gives an agent an MCP tool that pumps a deterministic 16 ms virtual frame clock, reports animating vs settled, and returns a screenshot at exactly the requested instant ('advance(16, screenshot) is a per-frame flipbook'). Input actions take settle:false so a triggered transient stays observable on the next advance. That is fixed 1-frame virtual stepping for agent perception, which is condition (c) of the proposed experiment. It is a UI toolkit, not Chromium, and has no adaptive step.

closest_prior_art.name: VGCP (Video Game Control Protocol)
closest_prior_art.overlap: MCP/TCP protocol for AI agents: the game starts paused, step advances exactly N ticks, screenshot returns a freshly drawn frame, and input is injected at the frozen instant. await_state and await_signal advance until a predicate holds, which is a semantic 'advance until event'. It does not detect events from pixel prediction error, and it targets Godot, not the web.

closest_prior_art.name: RimBridgeServer (step_game_ticks)
closest_prior_art.overlap: An MCP tool that advances a paused game by an exact number of ticks for an AI agent. Another instance of agent-controlled discrete stepping.

closest_prior_art.name: vlmkit PR #186: motion with the page clock held
closest_prior_art.overlap: VLM-oriented tooling that holds rAF, performance.now, Date and timers on a virtual clock from document start and advances it at 60 fps to sample script-driven motion for a VLM, at fixed instants (0/250/500/1000/2000 ms and animation start/mid/end). It records that a 500 ms carousel was missed by real-time rest captures. Its findings: 'what still moves with the clock held is video / an animated image / a worker', and under Chromium's virtual clock the GPU arm drew no rAF frame at all. This is directly relevant prior art and evidence on feasibility.

closest_prior_art.name: Swift Sampling: Selecting Temporal Surprises via Taylor Series (arXiv 2605.22678)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Taylor-expansion prediction of the feature trajectory, with frames chosen where the actual features diverge from the prediction. This is the same estimator, used offline on recorded video in VLM feature space.

closest_prior_art.name: VideoGameBench Lite (arXiv 2505.18134)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Pauses the emulator while the VLM thinks and observes only at step boundaries. Turns real time into turn-based play.

closest_prior_art.name: Adaptive Predictive Sampling and Communication for Real-time Monitoring (arXiv 2609.26493), plus the send-on-delta event-based sampling literature
closest_prior_art.overlap: Classical theory for the controller: pick the next sampling interval from local signal dynamics estimated from past samples, to hit a target reconstruction error, and sample only on significant deviation from prediction (send-on-delta). The adaptive near-Nyquist, constant-surprise-per-sample framing is well established here.

closest_prior_art.name: Adaptive step size control (embedded error estimators in ODE integrators)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The source of the controller law h_{n+1} = h_n * clamp(safety * (tol/e)^(1/p)). Textbook.

closest_prior_art.name: timesnap / timecut
closest_prior_art.overlap: Overrides Date, performance.now, rAF and timers in-page to capture web animations frame by frame at virtual times, slower than real time. Used for recording, not for agent perception.

closest_prior_art.name: Playwright Clock API (pauseAt / runFor)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Pause and tick-by-tick advance of a page's clock to observe animations at exact instants (tests and screenshots).

closest_prior_art.name: demo-reel deterministic compositor (beginFrame capture)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Combines setVirtualTimePolicy(pause) with HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame for exact committed frames. It documents that the compositor still runs on real time and that headed Chrome has no BeginFrameControl.

closest_prior_art.name: Learning Action Duration in Fighting Games (arXiv 2605.20911)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The agent picks how many frames to skip per action, a state-dependent temporal step. It is learned by RL, not error-controlled.

closest_prior_art.name: Real-Time Reasoning Gym / AgileThinker (arXiv 2511.04898, ICLR 2026)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The opposite design point: the environment keeps evolving during deliberation. It frames the same latency gap this idea tries to dodge by pausing.

entries.what_remains_new: What remains is narrow and engineering-level: closing the loop with a pixel-space prediction-error step-size controller on Chromium's own virtual clock, so the stepping interval shrinks after a surprise. That comes with an agent-facing 'advance(until=surprise), then hold on that exact frame; act_at(current virtual instant)' primitive for a browser. I found nothing that adapts h online from the Taylor-extrapolation residual of a cheap luma signature during live virtual-time stepping. Swift Sampling does it offline. WaterUI, VGCP and vlmkit step with fixed or user-chosen h. VGCP's await_state stops on a semantic predicate, not on visual surprise. ABP pauses only at action boundaries. Most of the claimed gain comes from parts that already exist: pausing removes reaction latency (ABP, VGB Lite, VGCP), and frame-exact stepping on a virtual clock catches short events (WaterUI, vlmkit, timesnap). The novel part is the adaptive controller, and it only buys frame efficiency after the first sample in an event. It cannot improve first detection beyond what uniform h = h_max already gives (see technical_flaws).
entries.technical_flaws_found:
1) The adaptive controller does not help first detection. The ODE analogy fails at the key step. An embedded RK integrator rejects a step and retries it with a smaller h. Here a step cannot be rejected, because virtual time cannot be rewound without a full page snapshot or replay. A 120 ms flash on a static background has no smooth precursor, so e_n stays at noise level until the flash is actually sampled. Meanwhile the controller grows h toward h_max. If h_max > 120 ms, any flash that falls wholly between two samples is lost, and recall is about 120/h_max. That is the same aliasing bound as uniform sampling at h_max. To get 98% recall you need h_max <= ~118 ms. Uniform h = 100 ms already gives 100% recall at 10 frames/s, about 17% of the 60 fps frame count, which already meets the '<=20% of fixed 1-frame' target with no controller. So the stated falsifier ('controller recall at a fixed budget no better than uniform') is likely to trigger for detection recall. The controller's real benefit is only intra-event refinement (onset and offset timing, motion within an event). Calling it 'near-Nyquist' is also loose: Nyquist needs bandlimited signals, and step flashes are not bandlimited. The honest bound is h_max <= min event duration.

2) Chromium virtual time does not cleanly govern rendering. Prior art reports that the compositor keeps running on real time under setVirtualTimePolicy: compositor-thread CSS transform/opacity animations, scroll animations, GIF/APNG and image decode (demo-reel issue #13, vlmkit #186). vlmkit also saw that under Chromium's virtual clock the GPU path drew no rAF frame at all. rAF depends on BeginFrames, which virtual time does not issue in headful or new-headless Chrome. Page.startScreencast only emits on new compositor frames, so 'screencast latest' will return stale frames while time is paused. Exact committed frames need HeadlessExperimental.beginFrame, which works only in chrome-headless-shell (old headless) with --enable-begin-frame-control and --run-all-compositor-stages-before-draw. This repo's headful and new-headless paths cannot use it. The fallback is in-page clock override (timesnap-style), which misses compositor animations and video.

3) The virtual-time budget has awkward semantics for tiny steps. When the page is idle, virtual time fast-forwards to the next timer, and budgetExpired fires based on the virtual task scheduler, not on frame production. A 16.7 ms budget does not guarantee that exactly one rAF or paint happened. Every step needs its own begin-frame plus capture handshake, and screenshot cost of about 30 to 100 ms per step makes the proposed '80 ms overhead' bound tight. At 10 steps per virtual second, 60 s of virtual time costs roughly 30 to 60 s of wall-clock, which is fine. At 60 steps per second it costs 2 to 5 minutes.

4) The 16x16 luma signature has limited sensitivity. At 1280x720 each cell is 80x45 px. A small or low-contrast target changes one cell's mean by only (area fraction) x contrast, which can sit under the noise floor that sets e_n. The 98% recall claim depends on target size and contrast, and a finer or tile-max signature may be needed.

5) The in-window click hit-rate result is nearly guaranteed, so it is not evidence for the controller. Once the page is paused on the event frame, the model's 2 s deliberation costs zero virtual time, and the hit rate is about 100% of detected targets. That is exactly the ABP / VGB-Lite / VGCP property. Input dispatched while virtual time is paused may also be queued until the next advance, so act_at needs a small advance after dispatch to deliver the event, and that slightly shifts the click instant.

6) Out-of-scope items still leak in. HTMLMediaElement, Web Workers, WebSockets, WebRTC and server-timed content are not governed by virtual time, so such pages show 'motion with the clock held' and break the frozen-world assumption.

entries.title: Sham-controlled interventional diff (SCID): measure what an action did by subtracting a measured null model of the page's own motion, with optional time clamping
entries.hypothesis: Naive before/after diffs, and VLM before/after judges given two screenshots, give false 'the action had an effect' verdicts on pages with autonomous motion. At a fixed true-positive rate, SCID cuts the false-positive rate on no-op actions by at least 3x. SCID with clamping also raises the detection rate for small (16-32 px) delayed effects that land inside animated regions, which the unclamped version reports as undecidable. The hypothesis is falsified if unclamped SCID does not beat the naive diff on false-positive rate at matched true-positive rate, or if clamping suppresses real effects, i.e. delayed setTimeout responses no longer appear within budget W.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: control-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: The closest prior work is GUI action-effect verification from before/after screenshots: VisCritic (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.24525), Evidence-First Reflection with action-induced visual differences and SoM-marked changed regions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24015), and 'Don't Act Blindly' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.05477). From their abstracts (I did not read the full papers, so this is unverified), they separate action-relevant from irrelevant changes with a model that judges two frames. None of them measures a per-region null model of autonomous change, and none intervenes on the page clock. The second neighbour is visual regression testing, e.g. Playwright's screenshot animations:'disabled' and Percy/Chromatic freezing. That freezes animations to make two renders comparable. It runs no sham control, gives no per-tile significance or power estimate, and is not used inside an agent's action loop to produce a residual-only percept. The third neighbour is WMA (ICLR 2025) and Code2World, which predict the transition with a learned model. SCID instead measures the transition causally and makes the null prediction exact by clamping. The CDP facts are from the protocol docs: virtual time replaces timers and rAF, with policies pause, advance and pauseIfNetworkFetchesPending and a budget (https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/tot/Emulation/). I have not verified whether virtual time freezes CSS animations in headful Chrome, which is why Animation.setPlaybackRate(0) is applied as well and the sham windows measure how complete the clamp is.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate, unvalidated: a false-positive rate on no-op actions of about 30-60% for the naive diff on this page, against under 10% for SCID unclamped. Effect-region IoU of at least 0.5 for small badges outside animated regions. Clamping should turn most badges inside animated regions from undecidable into detected. The cost is about K*W, roughly 1.8 s of sham observation, paid once per layout and amortised over later actions. The percept for the model shrinks from a full screenshot (about 1-1.8k tokens) to one or two crops (about 100-300 tokens) when the effect is small.
entries.experiment_required: Build one pytest-httpserver page with a carousel advancing every 800 ms (setInterval), a CSS spinner, a rAF particle canvas, a looping <video> generated by the existing test fixtures, and 24 buttons. Twelve buttons are no-ops. Twelve toggle a 20x20 px badge somewhere else on the page, half immediately and half after a 150 ms setTimeout, and a third of the badges sit inside the carousel or canvas area. Click each button 5 times through HumanInput and record the screencast frames, so ground truth is known. Compare (a) a naive pre/post tile diff with a threshold, (b) SCID unclamped with K = 3, and (c) SCID clamped. Optionally add (d) Claude given the pre and post screenshots and asked 'did the click change anything, and where'. Metrics: ROC-AUC and false-positive rate at 90% true-positive rate for effect vs no-op, IoU of the effect region with the badge rectangle, the share of trials reported undecidable, and the wall-time overhead of the sham windows. Run time is under 10 minutes on CPU, and every arm except (d) uses zero model tokens.
entries.mechanism:
Problem: on a live page, pre/post screenshot diffs mix the action's effect with autonomous dynamics such as carousels on setInterval, CSS spinners, rAF canvases, looping <video>, tickers and lazy ads. Eyes.next() handles this only for feed flicks, by checking the item id. SCID treats the browser as a plant with an exogenous disturbance and estimates the action's effect as a controlled experiment.

Inputs: the Page.screencast stream page.py already consumes (zero model tokens), cut into a tile grid. Use T = 32x18 tiles, each with an 8x8 mean-luma signature (an extension of page.signature), so n = 576 tiles. Also the DOMSnapshot bounds the repo already fetches.

(1) Null model. Before acting, run K sham windows (K = 3), each of length W, where W is the action's settle window (default 600 ms). No input is sent. A tile counts as changed in a window when its signature distance exceeds tau, after global translation is removed with perceive.scroll_estimate. For each tile i, estimate its autonomous change rate with a Beta(0.5, 0.5) posterior: p_i = (c_i + 0.5)/(K + 1). Cache p_i per URL and layout hash; refresh it when the layout hash changes.

(2) Optional clamp to raise statistical power. Send Animation.setPlaybackRate(0) to hold CSS and WAAPI animations, pause the attended media (the retina already has hold), and send Emulation.setVirtualTimePolicy({policy: 'pause'}). The action window is then run under policy 'advance' with budget W, so timers the action schedules (debounced menus, setTimeout reveals) still fire. Autonomous setIntervals fire too, so the sham windows run under the same clamp policy and budget. The null model always matches the regime of the action window. Restore everything afterwards.

(3) Action window. Dispatch the action, collect frames for W, and record a per-tile change indicator x_i. Tile surprise is s_i = -log p_i if x_i = 1, else 0. A tile is an effect tile when x_i = 1 and p_i < alpha/n (Bonferroni, alpha = 0.05), or alternatively under Benjamini-Hochberg. Effect tiles are merged into connected components to give effect regions.

(4) Power check. For every tile the action changed, the probability of detecting it is 1[p_i < alpha/n]. If the only changed tiles sit in high-p_i regions, the verdict is 'undecidable: effect would be masked by autonomous motion', not 'no effect'.

Outputs: a verdict in {effect, no_effect, undecidable}; effect-region bounding boxes in viewport coordinates, the DOM nodes that intersect them, and full-resolution crops of only those regions; and the masked fraction sum_i p_i / n. Because the clamped null predictor is 'nothing changes', the crops are exactly the action's prediction residual. That is a residual-only percept a closed API model can consume, with no learned world model.

closest_prior_art.name: Bellemare, Veness, Bowling - Investigating Contingency Awareness Using Atari 2600 Games (AAAI 2012); follow-up Choi et al. Contingency-Aware Exploration (ICLR 2019)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Same causal question: which screen regions are under the agent's control and which change on their own. They use a learned per-pixel predictive model and a Bayesian filter to find 'contingent regions'. SCID's per-tile Bayesian change rate for autonomous motion against action-window change is the same decomposition into controllable and uncontrollable pixels. The differences are that SCID measures it with sham windows instead of learning it, and works on web pages instead of Atari. Follow-up: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01483

closest_prior_art.name: Evidence-First Reflection (EFR): Reflection with Action-Induced Visual Differences for Desktop GUI Agents
closest_prior_art.overlap: Algorithm C.1 is the naive arm of SCID inside an agent loop: a grayscale pre/post absolute diff, a threshold, a mask, merging of nearby boxes and dropping tiny regions, then SoM-marked crops. Autonomous changes such as clocks and 'animation updates' are filtered by a VLM prompt that tags regions as [Noise]. It has no no-action baseline and no time control. This confirms the gap SCID targets, but the pipeline from pixel diff to changed-region crops for an agent already exists.

closest_prior_art.name: auto-mobile PR #6217: flag animating apps (TouchLatencyTracker)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Runs an explicit no-input idle window before injecting a tap. If frames render during it, the sample is marked 'animating' and discounted, and an explicit animating/undecidable flag is reported instead of a misleading result. This is a sham control plus an undecidable verdict for GUI input effects. It is global (frame counters), not per-region, and it measures latency rather than localising effects.

closest_prior_art.name: lbframe/agent-visual-diff PR #1: ignore/mask regions for known-dynamic areas
closest_prior_art.overlap: A visual diff tool aimed at agents. Dynamic zones such as carousels and marquees were found empirically from repeated captures of the same section 3 s apart, then masked. That is an informal null model from repeated captures. The masks are hand-entered and there is no statistics.

closest_prior_art.name: DBAR - Deterministic Browser Agent Runtime
closest_prior_art.overlap: Uses Emulation.setVirtualTimePolicy inside a browser-agent step loop to freeze Date.now, timers and rAF, and captures a screenshot, DOM and AX tree at each step boundary for comparison. This is SCID's clamp component, already used in an agent action loop, but for replay determinism rather than effect estimation.

closest_prior_art.name: Playwright toHaveScreenshot (animations: 'disabled', two-consecutive-screenshot stabilisation)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Freezes CSS animations, transitions and WAAPI. It also repeats captures until two consecutive screenshots match, which is a crude null-stability check before comparing. Argos (https://argos-ci.com/blog/screenshot-stabilization) and Chromatic SteadySnap do the same and also flag flaky snapshots across runs.

closest_prior_art.name: Microsoft US7296184B2 - Masking dynamic regions in a UI to enable testing of UI consistency
closest_prior_art.overlap: Masks UI regions that change on their own to reduce false positives in snapshot diffs, including a 'bulk' mask added at the coordinates of an animation found in difference snapshots. The masks are manual or semi-manual, and there is no significance test or clock control.

closest_prior_art.name: PUSV in 'Temporal UI State Inconsistency in Desktop GUI Agents' (TOCTOU)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Calibrates a global screenshot-diff threshold for an agent loop from measured benign no-input activity (under 0.05% of pixels per second), then sets tau = 0.2%. This is a global null model, not a per-region one.

closest_prior_art.name: Puppeteer issue #511: pause all animations via Animation.setPlaybackRate(0)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The CDP Animation.setPlaybackRate(0) clamp for deterministic screenshots is long-standing folklore.

closest_prior_art.name: DynamicUI - Benchmarking and Improving GUI Agents in High-Dynamic Environments
closest_prior_art.overlap: Agents on highly dynamic GUIs, using video between actions with clustering and captioning. It does not separate autonomous changes from action-caused ones, so it is a neighbour and supports the claim of a gap.

entries.what_remains_new:
Each part has prior art: no-input sham windows (auto-mobile, agent-visual-diff's repeated captures, PUSV's global calibration), animation and timer clamping inside an agent loop (DBAR, Playwright, Argos), pre/post pixel diff to region crops for an agent (EFR), and the causal split into controllable and autonomous regions (Bellemare 2012 contingency awareness, learned). I found no work that combines all of the following:
(a) A per-tile autonomous-change rate measured by sham windows, used as an explicit null hypothesis for a web agent's action, instead of a VLM noise tag or a hand-made mask.
(b) A regime-matched null: sham windows run under the same virtual-time 'advance' budget and the same playback clamp as the action window, so the clamp only has to be measured, not trusted to be complete.
(c) A three-way verdict, effect / no_effect / undecidable, based on detectability per tile ("the effect would be masked by autonomous motion"), in place of a binary diff.
(d) Using the clamped residual crops as the model's only percept to save tokens.
Treat this as an engineering synthesis and a benchmark contribution, not a new principle. The likely publishable part is the ablation of SCID against EFR-style diffs and VLM judges on pages with autonomous motion and known ground truth.
entries.technical_flaws_found:
1. The significance test as written can never fire. With K = 3 and the Beta(0.5, 0.5) posterior, p_i = (c_i + 0.5)/(K + 1) is at least 0.125. The Bonferroni threshold is alpha/n = 0.05/576, about 8.7e-5, so no tile can ever pass. Benjamini-Hochberg fails the same way, since its smallest threshold is also alpha/n for rank 1. Every changed tile would therefore be 'undecidable'. Reaching p_i below 8.7e-5 would need roughly 5,800 sham windows. Ways to fix it:
- In the clamped regime, treat the null as deterministic: any change in a tile with c_i = 0 counts as an effect, and the sham windows only verify that the clamp holds.
- Test connected regions instead of tiles, which reduces the multiple-comparison count and pools evidence across tiles.
- Use a spatial or Markov random field prior, or a likelihood ratio, against the measured rate.
- Drop the per-tile frequentist correction entirely.
The '>= 3x lower false-positive rate' hypothesis cannot be tested until this is fixed.

2. Virtual time is not cleanly reversible. CDP has no 'disable virtual time' command. Once enabled, the renderer stays on the virtual clock, and policy 'advance' fast-forwards to the next delayed task rather than tracking wall-clock time. 'Restore everything afterwards' is probably impossible in the same renderer. That matters for headful co-browsing, where the human shares the tab, and for Date.now-dependent sites such as auth token expiry and rate limiters. This is my understanding of the protocol and the known Chromium behaviour; I did not verify it in this run. Separately, virtual time has historically been reliable mainly in headless mode with BeginFrame control.
