In headful Chrome, compositor-thread animations run on real time, and <video> playback does not follow virtual time. The proposal does acknowledge this.

3. Screencast under virtual time. Page.startScreencast only emits frames when the compositor produces them. During a fast-forwarded 'advance' budget, intermediate frames may be skipped. Transient effects, such as a toast that appears and disappears within W, can be missed. Network requests keep running in real time and, unless pauseIfNetworkFetchesPending is used, can land outside the budget.

4. Stationarity. Caching p_i per URL and layout hash assumes the autonomous dynamics are stationary. Carousels that stop on hover, ads that rotate in, and video that starts after an interaction all break that assumption. Hovering over the target before clicking can itself change the autonomous dynamics, for example by pausing a carousel. That shows up as a spurious effect in the very region the hypothesis cares about.

5. Global effects such as layout shifts, accordion reflow, and scroll anchoring move many tiles at once. Removing global translation with scroll_estimate will not cancel partial reflow, so effect regions can become large and the claimed token savings disappear. That is correct as an effect verdict but weak as localisation.

6. A tile signature of 8x8 mean luma per 40x40 px tile, at 1280x720, may not register a 20x20 badge whose colour has similar luminance, or a text-only change. The detection floor needs calibrating, or the signature should include chroma or edge energy.

Even with these issues, the core idea is sound: run a sham control under the same clamp as the action window, and report 'undecidable' when the effect would be masked by autonomous motion.

entries.title: Decoder-clock servo: drive video.playbackRate (and surprise-triggered rewinds) as the retina's sensor-rate actuator, with a guaranteed sample density
entries.hypothesis: On the repo's ground-truth test videos and a set of local reels (talking head, slideshow, static product shot with music, fast-cut montage), the servo cuts wall-clock time per watch by at least 40% at matched outputs. It keeps cut-detection F1 within 0.03 of a 1x watch, keeps the facility-location coverage F(S) of the chosen keyframes within 5%, and keeps transcript WER within 2 points, because speech is gated to <= 1.25x. The hypothesis is falsified if any of these holds: Chrome's decoder drops frames at r >= 2 so that the measured media-time sample density falls below 10 Hz; captureStream audio features become unusable at r != 1 (as reported for Firefox, where playbackRate does not apply to MediaStreamGraph); or the regressive saccade costs more wall time than it saves.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: control-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: Several neighbours exist. FFNet (Lan et al., CVPR 2018) and the collaborative multi-agent fast-forwarding work (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.17569, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.04437) learn to skip frames of a fully accessible offline file. Adaptive frame selection agents (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.20252) and ElasticPlay (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.06858) choose frames or summaries under a time budget. Human-facing adaptive playback speed (e.g. SmartPlayer, CHI 2009, which I did not re-verify) changes speed for a person watching. The repo's own vision/video.py seek-bisection needs random access to the media. None of these treats a third-party player's decode clock as an actuator in a closed loop. That loop has a sample-density guarantee derived from rVFC presentation, decoder-health feedback, an audio-intelligibility constraint, and surprise-triggered rewinds, and it works on streaming or MSE media where seeking ahead is unavailable or expensive. Surveyed work (LivingScreen, AOI) treats watch time as fixed wall time spent at 1x. This idea changes the exchange rate between media time observed and wall time spent. Browser facts: Chrome throws outside [0.0625, 16] and Gecko mutes audio outside [0.25, 4.0] (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLMediaElement/playbackRate). Chrome's muting range and whether captureStream follows playbackRate are unverified, and the experiment measures both.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate: a 40-65% cut in wall time on low-surprise content (slideshows, static shots with music), and near 0% on dense montages, where the controller should hold r near 1. For a feed-browsing session this means roughly 1.5-2.5x more items observed per wall minute at equal per-item percept quality, which moves the LivingScreen-style success-versus-watch-time frontier. If Chrome drops frames above 2x, the gain is capped at about 2x.
entries.experiment_required: Add a test to tests/ci/test_eyes.py that uses the existing ground-truth generated videos (known cut times, a tone and a beat track), plus a TTS speech clip, all served by pytest-httpserver. Sweep fixed rates r in {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8} and measure for each: rVFC presented frames per media second, droppedVideoFrames, cut F1 against ground truth, keyframe coverage F(S) relative to 1x, the band-spectrum correlation of hearing features against 1x, and Whisper WER at 1 / 1.25 / 1.5 / 2x. Then run the closed-loop servo against fixed 1x and measure wall time to the bored stop and the same quality metrics. This takes about 5 minutes of CPU and no model tokens. Check headless and headful separately, because R_disp and the decoder path differ.
entries.mechanism:
retina.js samples the attended <video> at opts.fps = 10 per second of MEDIA time, via requestVideoFrameCallback, which fires once per presented frame. Each sample carries both mediaTime and the wall timestamp (the frames tuple stores mt and now). The compositor presents at most about R_disp = 60 frames per wall second. At playbackRate r, a video of native rate f therefore delivers min(f, R_disp/r) presented frames per media second. With f = 30 and R_disp = 60, the 10 Hz media-time grid is fully preserved up to r = 6. Watching low-information stretches at 1x wastes wall-clock time with no gain in what the retina sees.

The servo closes the loop on the decoder clock, once per retina batch (k, every 200 ms).

Sensor: the luma prediction residual. With a second-order extrapolation on the 16x16 grid, ghat_t = 2 g_{t-1} - g_{t-2}, e_t = mean|g_t - ghat_t|. Its surprise rate per wall second is s_k = r_k * (count of e_t > theta_e per media second), where theta_e is the existing MAD-adaptive cut floor reused.

Actuator: v.playbackRate, set from the isolated world where the retina already holds the element.

Control law (log-domain proportional): r_{k+1} = clip(r_k * exp(-kappa (s_k - s*)), 1, r_max,k), with kappa = 0.5 and s* = 1 surprise per wall second.

Constraints:
(a) Sample-density bound: r_max = min(16, R_disp_measured / f_needed). R_disp is measured from rVFC presentedFrames per wall second, and f_needed = opts.fps.
(b) Decoder health: if getVideoPlaybackQuality().droppedVideoFrames increases by more than 5% of the frames presented in the batch, set r_max *= 0.7.
(c) Hearing: when Silero VAD reports speech and ASR is requested, force r <= r_speech (1.25, a tunable), because Whisper accuracy falls with time compression. Non-speech hearing features are kept in media time, which the retina already does for audio hops with v.playbackRate. Onset and tempo statistics are divided by r.
(d) Regressive saccade: if a cut or a large residual is detected while r > 1.5, seek back by r * (flushMs + analysis lag) media seconds and replay that window at r = 1. Facility-location keyframes around the event are then drawn from dense samples.
(e) Restore the page's original playbackRate when the watch ends. Back off and report if the page's player keeps resetting the rate through ratechange events.

Outputs are unchanged (Sight, Hearing, Percept, with media-time axes) plus a rate trace. The 'bored' stop is evaluated in media time, so it still stops after the same amount of content, but reaches that point in less wall time.

closest_prior_art.name: Jump Cutter (WofWca), open-source browser extension, AGPL
closest_prior_art.overlap: This is the closest work. It runs a closed loop on the playbackRate of an arbitrary third-party page's <video> or <audio> element: it measures loudness through Web Audio and an AudioWorklet, raises playbackRate on silent stretches and lowers it when sound returns, using about 200 ms of lookahead. An experimental 'cloning' mode plays a hidden clone ahead of the target to log silent stretches, then speeds up or seeks through them. A MutationObserver re-attaches the controller to new media elements. What is missing: the sensor is audio silence, not a visual prediction residual; there is no rVFC sample-density bound, no decoder-health feedback and no rewind. Its consumer is a human, not a machine retina.

closest_prior_art.name: Silence Cut (Chrome extension) / Skip Silence (vantezzen)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Silence Cut speeds playback up to 16x on silent stretches of a third-party player and drops back to 1x before speech. Skip Silence (https://github.com/vantezzen/skip-silence) adapts its threshold to each video's noise floor, which is the same idea as an adaptive theta, and uses an audio lookahead. Both show that driving playbackRate as an actuator on someone else's player is shipped practice.

closest_prior_art.name: SmartPlayer: User-Centric Video Fast-Forwarding (Cheng, Luo, Chen, Chu, CHI 2009)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Adjusts playback speed continuously from scene complexity and semantic events, using a 'slow down near interesting areas' metaphor. This is the content-adaptive speed law, built for human viewers.

closest_prior_art.name: US6760536B1 - Fast video playback with automatic content based variable speed
closest_prior_art.overlap: A patented variable playback speed driven by content within each shot: slow at a shot's start, accelerating as the shot goes on. This is close to 'slow down after a cut/surprise, speed up through redundancy'. Related patents: US11929096 / US12198726 'Content-based adaptive speed playback' (https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11929096) and US9741392B2 (https://patents.google.com/patent/US9741392B2/en).

closest_prior_art.name: DIDA: Dynamic Information-Density-Aware Video Playback Scaling (Alan She, TDCommons defensive publication, June 2026)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Sets a playback rate per segment (0.75x to 3.0x) from an entropy-based density score, visual frame classification, speech rate and silence. Rate changes are smoothed over a 500 ms window. Published as a defensive disclosure, and aimed at human viewers.

closest_prior_art.name: AIx Speed: Playback Speed Optimization Using Listening Comprehension of Speech Recognition Models (Kawamura & Rekimoto, AHs 2023 / UIST 2022 adjunct)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Directly covers constraint (c). It uses an ASR model's recognition score as the intelligibility limit and pushes speech speed, down to phoneme level, as high as the recognizer can still follow. The idea's 'gate speech to r <= 1.25 because Whisper degrades' is a coarser version of this.

closest_prior_art.name: Content-Aware Playback Speed Control for Low-Latency Live Streaming of Sports (CAPSC, MMSys 2021)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Controls the player's playback rate in closed loop from content features in live streaming. The objective is latency and buffer rather than perception, but it is still a content-driven servo on the decode clock.

closest_prior_art.name: FFNet (Lan et al., CVPR 2018), Distributed Multi-agent Video Fast-forwarding, Adaptive Video Understanding Agent
closest_prior_art.overlap: A machine consumer choosing frames or skips adaptively under a budget, on offline files (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.04437 and AVUA). This is the 'agent decides temporal sampling density' half of the idea, without the playbackRate actuator.

closest_prior_art.name: Milanfar et al., An Adaptive Framework for Image and Video Sensing
closest_prior_art.overlap: An adaptive sensor that sets its temporal sampling rate from content measured on each frame. This is the general 'sensor-rate actuator driven by scene content' control idea, from computational imaging.

closest_prior_art.name: Chrome media updates 63/64 (WSOLA, no audio muting) and Mozilla bug 1517199 (playbackRate ignored for captureStream / MediaStreamGraph)
closest_prior_art.overlap: These settle two of the idea's 'unverified' browser facts. Since Chrome 64, audio is time-stretched with WSOLA and is not muted across the 0.0625-16 range (it used to be muted outside 0.5-4). Firefox ignores playbackRate on captured streams (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1517199) and its audio skips above 2x (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1427267).

entries.technical_flaws_found:
1. The 'works on streaming where seeking ahead is unavailable' claim is half wrong. On live streams (HLS/DASH live, Twitch), r > 1 only catches up to the live edge and then stalls. No fast-forward is possible past real time, so the gain on live is zero. On VOD over MSE, the network must deliver r times the bitrate. ABR players (YouTube, shaka, hls.js) respond by dropping rendition quality or rebuffering, so the servo trades wall time for resolution or stalls. Buffer health (v.buffered ahead of currentTime, 'waiting' events) has to be a constraint, and the idea leaves it out.

2. Sample-density bound. Composition is capped near the display rate, so at r = 6 with a 30 fps source Chrome's video renderer discards about 2/3 of decoded frames before presentation. Whether those discards are counted in droppedVideoFrames is implementation-specific. Constraint (b) may therefore not fire even when frames are lost, and presentedFrames per wall second is the better signal. Headless Chrome is another problem: begin-frame and vsync scheduling can be throttled or virtualized, so R_disp measured headless does not transfer to headful. Background or occluded tabs throttle rVFC heavily.

3. Chrome facts are already settled. Since Chrome 64 audio is not muted anywhere in [0.0625, 16]; it is WSOLA time-stretched with preservesPitch on by default. Spectral and band features therefore survive approximately, but WSOLA artifacts grow above about 3-4x, and onset and tempo features stay in wall time, hence the divide-by-r. In Firefox, captureStream ignores playbackRate (bug 1517199), so the audio path breaks there.

4. The controlled variable is poorly motivated. A setpoint of s* = 1 surprise per wall second assumes downstream cost scales with wall time per surprise. The retina already samples on a fixed media-time grid, so a surprise at r = 4 is sampled as densely as one at r = 1. The only real reasons to slow down are denser-than-grid frames for keyframe selection, and audio and ASR, which the rewind and the speech gate already handle. A simpler bang-bang policy (r_max until an event, then rewind and replay at 1x) probably dominates the proportional law. There is also limit-cycle risk: kappa = 0.5 in the log domain with 200 ms batches, plus seek-induced residual spikes after each rewind, can oscillate unless rewind windows are masked from the sensor.

5. Short reels (15-60 s) dominate feed browsing. There, page load, autoplay negotiation and the bored-stop threshold dominate wall time, so the 1.5-2.5x items-per-minute estimate is optimistic. Many reel players also loop, or reset playbackRate on ratechange or loadedmetadata, which the idea does acknowledge with back-off.

6. The Whisper gate at 1.25x is conservative and empirically under-founded. AIx Speed shows ASR tolerates much higher local speedups on non-dense speech. A fixed cap leaves gain on the table, though it is safe.

The mechanism is implementable and will likely give 1.5-3x wall-time savings on static or slideshow VOD served locally, the test setting. The hypothesis's 40% figure is plausible for that setting but not for live or ABR-streamed web media.

entries.title: Armed reflexes with plant dead-time identification: model-authored numeric guards evaluated in-page every frame, fired with a Smith-predictor lead
entries.hypothesis: For a 40 px target moving at 200, 600 and 1200 px/s on a local page, a reactive VLM-coordinate tap misses almost always above 200 px/s (miss of about v x 0.5-2 s). An armed reflex without lead has a miss of about v*D, where D is predicted at 25-60 ms on local Chromium, so it misses frequently at 1200 px/s. With Smith-predictor lead the hit rate is at least 90% at all three speeds. For transient targets (a toast with an Undo button visible for 400 ms, a key prompt with a 250 ms window), armed reflexes succeed at least 95%. The hypothesis is falsified if the lead variant does not beat the no-lead variant at 1200 px/s, meaning dead-time jitter or binding latency dominates, or if Event Timing cannot attribute CDP-dispatched input reliably enough to estimate D.
entries.originating_agent: Round 9 research workflow, scientist lens: control-theorist
entries.supporting_evidence: The closest work is AAPT, pre-compiled policy trees (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.28399). It pre-plans guarded branches with deadlines, but its guards are routed by a lightweight multimodal model decode (about 59 tokens per call) after a 30 FPS pixel-diff gate, it executes through pyautogui, and its authors state there is no compensation for moving targets. Here the guards are compiled numeric predicates evaluated in-page per presented frame with no model call, and the browser's input-to-present dead time is identified online with Event Timing and corrected with a Smith predictor. SikuliX-style wait(image)-then-click is a template wait with no tracking, latency model or lead. Latency compensation for moving-target selection is well studied for human players (Claypool et al., https://web.cs.wpi.edu/~claypool/papers/delay-motion/paper.pdf; geometric compensation, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3290605.3300790), but not as plant identification inside a browser-agent harness. The surveys list as an open gap that no system decouples a fast local reflex controller from the VLM planner for web canvas (AOI limitations, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29472; WebGames, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18356). Scope: this is meant for the user's own or test pages, single-player web apps and time-limited UI elements. It is not for multiplayer games, and it involves no human-imitation of timing.
entries.estimated_upside: Estimate: at 1200 px/s, B hits about 30-50% and C about 85-95%, if sigma_D is below 8 ms on local Chromium, which is unverified. Transient-target success near 100% for B and C, against about 0-30% for A on 250-400 ms windows. Planner cost: one VLM call to arm, not N observe-act calls, so token use per timed interaction drops by about 1-2 orders of magnitude relative to polling loops. No gain on events that cannot be enumerated in advance; that remains AAPT's failure case too.
entries.experiment_required: Build a pytest-httpserver page with three parts. (i) A 40 px disc moving on a canvas via rAF, with randomised constant-velocity and bouncing trajectories at 200, 600 and 1200 px/s; hits are logged by the page. (ii) A 'toast' with an Undo button that appears at random times for 400 ms. (iii) A key prompt with a 250 ms window. Arms: A, a reactive loop (retinat_look, then compute the coordinate, then tap), timing only, with a scripted LLM stub per CLAUDE.md test rules. B, an armed reflex without lead. C, an armed reflex with Dhat lead. 50 trials per cell. Also log the Dhat distribution in headless and headful, and verify it independently by comparing the page's logged pointerdown timestamp with the CDP dispatch time after clock sync. This takes under 10 minutes and uses no model tokens for arms B and C.
entries.mechanism:
Every observe-act loop is too slow for sub-300 ms events. AOI samples at about 3 Hz, and a reactive VLM loop measured about 567 ms p50 in AAPT. The fix here is to split the controller in two. The slow VLM is the planner: it emits a reflex spec. A fast, model-free loop inside the page is the executor.

(1) Reflex spec, as a pydantic model the MCP tool retinat_arm accepts. trigger is a predicate in a small closed DSL over signals the retina already computes per frame or per rAF tick. Examples: region_luma(R) distance to template signature T < d; element_bbox(sel) enters zone Z; audio onset with band > b; cut; text appears in DOM region (MutationObserver). action is a tap, key or click at an aim point, which may be given relative to a tracked object. Also: deadline, max_fires, and a refractory period.

(2) Fast loop. retina.js (isolated world) evaluates the predicate on each rVFC or rAF tick at 60 Hz. Target position comes from getBoundingClientRect for DOM targets, or from 16x16 template correlation on drawImage of an origin-clean canvas or video. An alpha-beta (or constant-acceleration Kalman) filter tracks position and velocity, xhat and vhat.

(3) Plant identification. Trusted input must come from CDP, so the loop is page -> binding -> Python -> Input.dispatch* -> renderer -> handler -> paint. Its dead time D is identified online. Clock sync between Python and page performance.now uses NTP-style minimum-RTT over the binding. For each dispatched input, the Event Timing API (PerformanceObserver type 'event', durationThreshold 16) records the event's startTime and processingStart and its next-paint duration. D_i = (startTime - t_trigger_page) + render-to-present, where render-to-present comes from the next rVFC or rAF timestamp. A running median Dhat and MAD sigma_D are kept. Dhat is also exposed as a measured property of the plant.

(4) Smith-predictor lead. The loop fires when the predicted target position at t + Dhat, xhat + vhat*Dhat (+ 0.5*ahat*Dhat^2), falls within the tolerance of the aim point, not when the current position does. The predicted miss is then about |v|*sigma_D instead of |v|*D. If |v|*sigma_D exceeds the target radius, the reflex abstains and reports 'unhittable at this jitter', which makes the latency/precision limit explicit.

(5) Report. Each firing returns trigger time, Dhat, predicted vs realised position, and an SCID-style tile check of whether the action had an effect. The planner gets one compact result per reflex.

closest_prior_art.name: AAPT: Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Pre-Compiled Policy Trees (arXiv 2607.28399)
closest_prior_art.overlap: The core planner/executor split. A frozen multimodal model, during idle time, authors a bounded tree of guards plus pre-authorized actions plus per-branch deadlines. Decisions are then routed off the slow path. Differences I confirmed from the HTML: guards are checked by a 64-token model decode (about 325 ms p50) after a 30 FPS pixel-diff gate, actions go out through pyautogui, and moving targets and latency prediction are not addressed. So 'arm a guarded action with a deadline' already exists. What is new here is that the guard is numeric with no model call, and that a lead is applied.

closest_prior_art.name: LagComp: Compensating Observation-to-Action Latency Through Latent Feature Forecasting
closest_prior_art.overlap: Almost the same control idea in robotics. It estimates end-to-end latency online from timestamped pipeline events, then forecasts forward by exactly that measured lag so the action matches the world when it executes. Reported success goes from 26% to 88% on interception and conveyor tasks. That is online dead-time identification plus predictive lead, minus the browser.

closest_prior_art.name: Reflex: Real-Time VLA Control through Streaming Inference (arXiv 2607.14695)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Forecasts state forward by the expected inference duration to avoid missing moving targets. Lookahead adapts to measured latency. Robotics only, not GUI or browser.

closest_prior_art.name: Fire-control lead prediction / predicted-intercept firing (US 4402251; US 6871439 target-actuated weapon)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Decades-old prior art for 'fire when the predicted target position at t+latency meets the aim point': tracker velocity and acceleration estimates, a straight-line or acceleration predictor, firing commands started at predicted intersection. Step (4) is this. It is not really a Smith predictor.

closest_prior_art.name: Game triggerbots with target leading (e.g. valorant-ai-panel, triggerbot repos)
closest_prior_art.overlap: Model-free pixel loops that auto-fire when the crosshair overlaps a target, with a 'leading target movement' option and configurable delay. Same fast-loop trigger plus lead pattern, done from screen capture with no planner. Weak academic standing, but clear prior practice.

closest_prior_art.name: Playwright page.waitForFunction(polling:'raf') / actionability stability checks
closest_prior_art.overlap: An in-page predicate evaluated on every rAF tick, followed by a trusted CDP click. That is the 'armed numeric guard evaluated per frame' part without the planner. It has no tracking or lead, and Playwright deliberately waits for elements to stop moving.

closest_prior_art.name: SikuliX Region.onAppear/observe
closest_prior_art.overlap: A background template-trigger handler that clicks event.match when a pattern appears (about 3 Hz scan, repeat/refractory via repeat(time)). Armed reflex with no tracking, no latency model and no lead.

closest_prior_art.name: Rapid-Reflex Async-Reflect / Reflex First, Reflect Later (arXiv 2506.07223); Latent Bridge (2606.24470); SPIKE (2605.18636)
closest_prior_art.overlap: A fast reflex layer decoupled from a slow LLM/VLM planner for dynamic and real-time game environments. Prior art for the controller split, though their fast layers are learned policies or small models, not compiled in-page predicates.

closest_prior_art.name: ActionEngine (arXiv 2602.20502); Web Agents Should Adopt Plan-Then-Execute (2605.14290)
closest_prior_art.overlap: A web/GUI agent compiles one program and then runs it deterministically with no further model calls (O(1) planning cost). Covers the 'one VLM call to arm, no N observe-act calls' cost argument.

closest_prior_art.name: Claypool, Game Input with Delay: Moving Target Selection; Lee et al. CHI 2019 Geometric Compensation
closest_prior_art.overlap: Models how latency and target speed drive moving-target selection error, and how to compensate for it. Human players only. Also see http://kuaa.net/publications/2019-GeometricCompensation.pdf.

closest_prior_art.name: google/latency-benchmark; Event Timing API spec; CDP-dispatched input yields Event Timing entries
closest_prior_art.overlap: Prior tooling for measuring browser input-to-paint latency by sending programmatic input and decoding the response. The W3C Event Timing spec (https://w3c.github.io/event-timing/) plus reports that Input.dispatchMouseEvent reliably produces Event Timing entries (https://dev.to/ikeshavvarshney/my-go-tests-never-executed-a-line-of-the-javascript-they-were-testing-4m0m) mean the measurement half is established practice, not invention.

entries.what_remains_new:
Every component exists already. Armed guarded actions with deadlines come from AAPT, SikuliX and Playwright raf-polling. A fast/slow split is standard in Reflex-First, SPIKE and Latent Bridge. Online latency identification plus a forecast-by-measured-lag lead is in LagComp and Reflex, and lead-on-predicted-intercept firing is old fire-control and triggerbot practice. What I could not find in any search is the specific combination inside a browser-agent harness:

(a) The VLM authors a typed reflex spec in a closed numeric-predicate DSL, which runs in an isolated world on every rVFC/rAF tick with zero model calls.
(b) The page→binding→Python→CDP Input→handler dead time is identified online, using Event Timing entries on the agent's own CDP-dispatched input plus NTP-style clock sync over the binding.
(c) A lead equal to that measured dead time is applied, with explicit abstention when |v|*sigma_D exceeds the target radius, reported as 'unhittable at this jitter'.

The abstention-with-jitter-bound report and the Event-Timing-based self-identification of the agent's own input plant are the most defensible novel pieces. Both are integration and engineering contributions, not a new control principle. A paper framed as 'first latency-compensated reflexes for web agents' would survive review only with the AAPT and LagComp comparisons stated up front.
entries.technical_flaws_found:
1) The dead time D is defined wrongly. A hit is decided when the page's pointerdown handler hit-tests against its current game state. That moment is processingStart, or more exactly the state from the last rAF before it. It is not the next present. Adding render-to-present (rVFC/rAF timestamp) to D over-leads by about 8-16 ms, which is 10-20 px at 1200 px/s, or half the 40 px disc diameter. The correct target is t_trigger → (processingStart, quantised to the game-state frame). For a page that checks hits against the displayed sprite, the relevant quantity is the age of the displayed frame, which is different again. D has to match the page's hit-test semantics, or the lead is biased.

2) 'Smith predictor' is the wrong name. A Smith predictor is a closed-loop structure: an internal delay-free plant model inside a feedback controller, corrected by the model-vs-plant output mismatch. This design is open-loop feedforward dead-reckoning, i.e. lead-computing fire control or predictive triggering. Calling it a Smith predictor overclaims and will be flagged by reviewers.

3) Frame quantisation sets a floor. The target only moves once per rAF (20 px per frame at 1200 px/s), and the guard is sampled at 60 Hz. So even with sigma_D = 0 there is up to ±half a frame of intrinsic phase error (about ±10 px) unless dispatch is scheduled sub-frame from Python using the predicted crossing time. Firing 'on the tick when the prediction is inside tolerance' wastes part of the tolerance budget.

4) The binding plus Python leg probably dominates jitter. Runtime.addBinding → CDP websocket → asyncio event loop (shared with bubus watchdogs, screencast frame decoding, GC) → Input.dispatchMouseEvent can show multi-ms to tens-of-ms tail jitter under load. The sigma_D < 8 ms assumption is the crux, and it is unverified. A median/MAD estimator also hides the heavy tails that cause the misses. Use p90/p95 for the abstain bound.

5) Template correlation on drawImage from a WebGL canvas returns a cleared buffer unless preserveDrawingBuffer is set, or unless the read happens in the same task after the page draws. rAF callback ordering between the page and the isolated world is not guaranteed. Cross-origin video or canvas taints the source and blocks getImageData. The canvas-target path will silently fail on many real pages.

6) Constant-velocity or constant-acceleration alpha-beta prediction breaks at bounces inside the D horizon (30-70 px at 1200 px/s). The ≥90% claim for bouncing trajectories needs either reflection-aware prediction or abstaining near walls.

7) The arm-A baseline is a strawman. A VLM tap at 0.5-2 s lag missing a target moving at more than 200 px/s is certain, so it tells you nothing. The informative comparisons are B vs C, plus an AAPT-style model-routed guard and a Playwright waitForFunction-raf-then-click baseline. Without those, the experiment cannot isolate the contribution against prior art.

8) Event Timing has a durationThreshold minimum of 16 ms and rounds duration to 8 ms. startTime for CDP input is the synthesized event timestamp. That timestamp may be set from the CDP 'timestamp' parameter or at browser-process receipt, so check whether it includes the Python→browser leg before using it to identify D. The proposed independent check (pointerdown timeStamp vs dispatch time after clock sync) is the right one and should be the primary estimator, not the secondary.
